PADLAB FIELD GUIDE · ANALOG STICKS

Stick drift, deadzones & the center point

By PadLab · Updated October 9, 2026

When your character walks or your camera turns without a touch, the controller may be reporting movement at rest. A stick drift test helps you see that signal before changing settings.

Start controller test →

Run a repeatable joystick drift test

  1. Connect your controller, open the gamepad tester and press a button. Confirm that the controller has a standard mapping.
  2. Move both thumbsticks around their full range. Release them gently and place the controller on a steady surface.
  3. Choose Run drift test. Keep the sticks untouched and the page visible during the three-second sample.
  4. Compare mean and peak offset, then repeat after moving and releasing the sticks from another direction.
  5. Export the report if you want a record. Use the same connection and browser when comparing later tests.

What the numbers mean

Each axis reports a normalized position from −1 to +1. For a standard controller, X represents horizontal movement and Y represents vertical movement. The center is approximately zero. A rightward movement usually makes X positive; downward movement usually makes Y positive.

PadLab calculates radial offset as sqrt(X² + Y²). An X value of 0.03 with Y at 0.04 gives a radial offset of 0.05, shown as 5%. A diagonal can exceed 100% when both axis values approach their limits. That alone is not a defect.

MeasurementWhat it tells you
Current offsetDistance from the center in the latest browser reading.
Mean radial offsetAverage distance from center across the sample. Opposing movements do not cancel out.
Peak radial offsetThe largest distance observed during the sample.
Mean X and YThe average direction of the center offset, included in the export.

Deadzone versus stick drift

A deadzone is a region where a game ignores small movements. It can hide a center offset, but it also changes how soon aiming or steering responds. A game's radial or axial deadzone may behave differently from the reference circle in this tester.

The shaded circle in PadLab is a visual guide. Moving the slider does not filter the raw numbers, repair drift or change firmware. There is no universal acceptable offset: evaluate the reading against your game’s settings and the behavior you actually experience.

What if the stick does not return to center?

Repeat the check with a USB data connection and verify that no remapping utility is adding a virtual controller. Check the manufacturer's documentation for supported firmware updates and calibration. If the same unwanted movement persists across games and devices, seek manufacturer support or a qualified repair service.

Hall effect and TMR describe sensing technologies. They do not guarantee a perfectly centered reading; springs, mechanics, firmware and calibration still affect the reported position.

Testing is not hardware calibration.

This tool observes values the browser exposes. It cannot access every sensor reading, certify a controller’s condition, or rewrite calibration data.

About the measurement

The sample lasts at least three seconds in a visible tab and collects readings at the interface’s refresh cadence. Repeated frames may contain the same hardware value. Results describe that sample, not USB polling frequency, long-term reliability or end-to-end input lag.

Technical reference: MDN’s Gamepad API guide. Also read our button and trigger test routine.

A worked example, not a hardware benchmark

The following numbers are illustrative. They explain the calculation and are not measured results from a controller.

SampleXYRadial offset
10.030.045%
2−0.03−0.045%

The mean radial offset is 5%, even though the mean X and mean Y are both zero. This is why averaging axis directions alone can hide movement. A 10% visual reference circle would contain both points, but that does not establish how a particular game filters its inputs.

Keep a comparison record

Take three separate samples after releasing the sticks from different directions. Save each export with the controller model, connection, browser and operating system. Compare repeatability rather than treating one brief peak as a fault. If the controller is missing or its mapping changes, resolve detection and mapping before comparing measurements.
